lead: Today’s readings are about a name and about rest. In Exodus Moses asks God for his name before he goes to the elders of Israel, and receives the great answer “I am who I am”. God makes himself known as the one who is, who was the God of the fathers, and who sees and will deliver. In the Gospel Jesus, the Son who alone knows the Father, speaks in his own person and says: “Come to me, all you that are weary… and I will give you rest.” The God who gave Moses his name now gives us himself, gentle and humble of heart. On this day the Church keeps the memorial of St Bonaventure, bishop and Doctor of the Church.

r.h: I AM has sent me to you
set: This is the second half of the scene at the burning bush. In vv. 1–12 God has called Moses and promised, “I will be with you.” Moses now raises a different difficulty. The Israelites in Egypt may ask which God has sent him, since the gods of Egypt were known by many names. Moses asks for the name that will make this God known.
str: v. 13: Moses asks what he is to say if they ask God’s name.
vv. 14–15: God gives the name, “I am who I am”, and tells Moses what to tell Israel; “This is my name forever.”
vv. 16–17: Moses is to assemble the elders and tell them of God’s visit and promise.
vv. 18–20: the elders and Moses will ask Pharaoh to let the people go three days’ journey to sacrifice; Pharaoh will not agree until God’s hand and wonders compel him.
kw: A Hebrew phrase that can also mean “I will be what I will be” or “I will be who I will be”. It is a name of presence, not of definition: God is the one who is there, who is with his people, and who cannot be reduced to an idol.

The four letters of the divine name, which sounds like the verb “to be”. Out of reverence the people of Israel do not pronounce it, and in reading Scripture they say Adonai, “Lord”. The Greek Old Testament puts Kyrios, “Lord”, and Christians follow the same practice.
God does not make a new beginning. He is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who kept the promises of old and will keep them now.
vv: God said to Moses, “I am who I am.”

The words are mysterious on purpose. God is not one being among many; he is the source of all being. The Greek Old Testament renders them “I am the One who is”, which later shaped Christian thought about God.
‘I am has sent me to you.’
The name is given for the sake of the people. They are not to be left with a distant power but with a God who is present and acts.
This is my name forever, and this my title for all generations.
The God who is with Moses is the same God who is with his people in every generation, including ours.
I know, however, that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand.
God does not hide the difficulty from Moses. He tells him in advance that Pharaoh will resist and that the deliverance will cost struggle.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in the revelation of the name God shows himself as the God who is always present, faithful and near, and that this name is mysterious and holy (CCC 205–206; 213). It notes also that the people of Israel do not pronounce the name out of reverence and that in the readings of Scripture the divine name is replaced by “Lord” (CCC 209). In the Gospel of John, Jesus speaks with the same words, “I am”, to reveal who he is (John 8:58; 18:5–6). Christian readers have long seen in the name an early announcement of the God of the Gospel, who is not a distant ruler but one who comes down to his people.

r.h: Come to me and I will give you rest
set: These three verses follow directly the thanksgiving of Jesus to the Father (11:25–27), where he says that the Son alone reveals the Father. Now the Son turns from the Father to the crowds. The Gospel of Matthew has just described cities that did not repent and people who found fault with both John and Jesus. In this setting Jesus makes his invitation without conditions: come.
str: v. 28: the invitation: come to me, you who are weary and heavy laden; I will give you rest.
v. 29: take my yoke and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; you will find rest for your souls.
v. 30: my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
kw: Not only sleep, but refreshment and peace. Rest in the Old Testament is a gift from God (Exodus 33:14), and a promise for those who walk in the ancient paths (Jeremiah 6:16, the words “find rest for your souls”).

The wooden bar that joined two animals to pull together. Teachers of Israel spoke of the “yoke” of the Law and of wisdom, as in Sirach 51:26. Jesus offers his own yoke, not a heavier load, but a new way of walking with him.
The word means good, kind, well fitted. A yoke that is “easy” is one made to fit the animal, so that it does not rub. Jesus’ commandments are fitted to us by grace.
vv: Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
The invitation is addressed to everyone. Jesus does not first ask for good works, but only that people come. He himself is the place of rest.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart
Jesus is a teacher, and to take his yoke is to become a disciple who learns. What he teaches is gentleness and humility, and he teaches it by being so himself.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

This does not mean that discipleship is without cost, for Jesus speaks elsewhere of the cross (16:24). It means that the one who carries it with Jesus is not alone and does not carry it by his own strength.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 29 in teaching that Christ is the model of holiness: “Learn from me” (CCC 459). St Augustine’s famous words, “our heart is restless until it rests in you” (Confessions, book 1), are often read as a commentary on Jesus’ promise of rest (in substance). The Church also remembers that the easy yoke is made light by grace, because the Holy Spirit pours the love of God into our hearts (Romans 5:5) and makes the commandments a way of freedom and joy.

qa: Why do the Church’s Bibles write “the Lord” where the Hebrew has the divine name?

Jewish tradition does not pronounce the holy name, out of reverence, and the Greek and Latin translations, and the Church after them, follow this practice. The Church keeps this practice, out of respect for the Jewish people who first received the name from God, and replaces it with “Lord” in the readings of Scripture (CCC 209).
rite: St Bonaventure was born about 1217 in Bagnoregio in Italy and studied and taught at the University of Paris. He became a Franciscan, and in 1257 was elected Minister General of the Order. He wrote the Itinerary of the Mind into God and a Life of St Francis. In 1273 he was made a cardinal and bishop of Albano, and he died on 15 July 1274 while taking part in the Second Council of Lyons. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1588 and is called the Seraphic Doctor. His life shows how study and prayer belong together: he held that the mind grows by learning and the heart grows by love, and that both lead to the God who invites the weary to rest.
study: God gives Moses a name which means presence. When have I most felt that God is “with me”?
Jesus says, “I am gentle and humble in heart.” Where might I let him teach me gentleness this week?
